frase_gancho.texto: A baby with a jaguar’s mouth, who has neither sex nor age.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the baby we move on to the old man. Step up to the Old God of Fire from Cuicuilco, one of the earliest gods known in Mesoamerica.

guion_corto.texto: This hollow figure of polished white clay comes from Tlapacoya, on the shore of the ancient Lake Chalco. It is a naked child, seated, with legs spread and hands resting on the ground, a shaved, bulging head, slanted eyes, swollen cheeks, and a mouth with thick lips turned down at the corners. It is the famous Olmec “baby-face,” and that mouth recalls the mouth of a feline. The curious thing is that this is not a real baby: it has no marked sex and no defined age. Specialists think it symbolizes a lineage, the purity of tender maize, or power inherited from the cradle.

guion_largo.texto:
On the hill of Tlapacoya, which was once an island in Lake Chalco, people have lived for a very long time: traces of hunters have been found here, remains of the first villages and, later, figures of this kind. That is why the site is so valuable: it is like a library where each layer of earth holds a different page of the valley’s history.

This figure is one of the most famous of the entire Preclassic. They are called “baby-face,” and it is easy to see why. They have a round head with no neck, a bulging forehead, eyes like slits, swollen cheeks, a plump body, and a mouth with a thick upper lip and corners turned down. But there is one detail that makes them even stranger: they almost never show signs of sex. They are neither boys nor girls, nor of any specific age. They are an idea.

What idea? There are several hypotheses here. One of the best known says that these faces represent the mythological children born of the union of a woman and a jaguar, a kind of original lineage. Another links them to water and rain, because among the Mesoamerican peoples the helpers of the rain god were small beings, like children, and it was believed that they brought the clouds. And others see them as a symbol of purity and of the tender maize that is just beginning to sprout. They probably held a little of everything.

The place where their importance is best understood is the Gulf Coast. When you reach the Gulf Coast Hall, look at the reproduction of the [Lord of Las Limas](mna_s08_senor_las_limas): a seated young man who holds in his arms one of these jaguar-children, limp, with a feline mouth and flame-shaped eyebrows. The scene seems to say that power, for the Olmec, came through caring for and guarding this mysterious child. Here, on the high plateau, the same child appears in clay, seated and awake.

This teaches something about how ideas traveled. Tlapacoya is hundreds of kilometers from the jungles where the Olmec style was born. And yet, there is the same face. We do not know whether there were merchants, priests, or artists who carried the images from one place to another, but what is clear is that the high plateau, a land of villages and farming, was open to a much larger world.

Notice also how it is made. It is a hollow piece, of polished white clay with a kind of light clay wash, and the head looks larger than normal, shaved, with a slight deformation. For the sculptor it was a way of emphasizing innocence and strength at once: the child who seems fragile but carries an immense power.

And to close with a curiosity: almost all the “baby-face” figures sit with their legs apart and their hands in front, as if waiting for someone to take them in their arms. See how much the story changes when you go back to the display case and look at it with that idea in mind: it is no longer a simple figurine, it is a question with legs.

texto: Find the mouth with thick lips turned down at the corners
Observe the shaved, bulging head, with no neck
Check that there are no features that indicate sex

texto.Culture: Preclassic of the Central Highlands, with Olmec influence

texto.pregunta: Myth: “Baby-face” figures are portraits of village children.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They are symbolic images in the Olmec style, with no defined sex or age, related to lineage, the jaguar, and fertility.
